stories.title: The Konkan Railway
stories.dek: Mumbai to Goa along a coast the British never built a railway on.
body: For most of the modern era, the Konkan coast between Mumbai and Mangaluru had no railway at all. The hills of the Western Ghats come right down to the sea here, cut by rivers every few kilometres, and even the British, who built most of India's network, never laid a line along it.

It took the Konkan Railway Corporation, led by the engineer E. Sreedharan, most of the 1990s to do it. The 756 km line needed more than 2,000 bridges and 92 tunnels, and was called the largest railway project of the century in Asia. Soft soil made some tunnels collapse again and again; seventy-four people died building the line. The first passenger train ran between Udupi and Mangaluru in March 1993, and the full route opened on 26 January 1998.

Riding it today, the train dives from tunnel to viaduct: the longest tunnel, at Karbude near Ratnagiri, runs for six and a half kilometres, and the Sharavathi bridge further south is two kilometres long. In the monsoon the whole coast turns green, and waterfalls pour off the cuttings beside the track.
Mumbai to Madgaon in Goa is the classic stretch: a morning train gets you there by afternoon.

stories.title: Past the Sea of Milk
stories.dek: A 310-metre waterfall, and a railway line that runs right across its face.
body: Dudhsagar means 'sea of milk'. The four-tiered waterfall on the Mandovi river, on the Goa–Karnataka border, drops 310 metres, one of the tallest in India, and it's at its fullest in and just after the monsoon.

The railway from the Goa coast up to Belagavi and Hubballi climbs through the Bhagwan Mahaveer Sanctuary and crosses in front of the falls on a bridge, so passengers see it from the train. You can't get off at the little Dudhsagar stop any more, and walking along the track is banned and dangerous: the train is the way to see it.
Trains from Vasco da Gama and Madgaon towards Hubballi make the climb through the Castle Rock ghat, with Dudhsagar on the way.

rides.label: Goa to Hubballi, past the falls

stories.title: Up to Ooty on a rack
stories.dek: India's only rack railway, and one of its slowest, most beautiful rides.
body: The Nilgiri Mountain Railway climbs from Mettupalayam, in the plains of Tamil Nadu, to Udhagamandalam (Ooty) in the Nilgiri hills. It took 45 years from the first plans in 1854 to the opening of the line to Coonoor in 1899; it reached Ooty in 1908.

Between Kallar and Coonoor the gradient is too steep for wheels alone, so the locomotive engages a toothed rack laid between the rails: it's the only rack railway in India. The steam engines on this section were built in Switzerland, and climbing, the train moves at about 15 km/h.
That's the point. The ride takes around five hours for 46 km, through tunnels and forest and past tea gardens, and in 2005 UNESCO added the line to the Mountain Railways of India World Heritage Site.

stories.title: The toy train to Darjeeling
stories.dek: Two feet of track, zig-zags, loops, and India's highest station.
body: Before 1881, getting from Kolkata to Darjeeling took five or six days, the last stretch by cart. The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, built between 1879 and 1881, runs 88 km from the plains near Siliguri up to about 2,200 metres, on track just two feet (610 mm) wide.

To climb that far on such a narrow line, it zig-zags: the train runs forward, reverses up the next leg, then runs forward again, gaining height along the hillside. It also turns full circles; the Batasia Loop, built in 1919, wraps the line around a garden with the Kanchenjunga range behind it.

Ghum, just before Darjeeling, is India's highest railway station at 2,260 m (not the world's highest, whatever some brochures say). In 1999 the DHR became the first railway in India to be named a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

stories.title: Kalka to Shimla, through 102 tunnels
stories.dek: The narrow-gauge line built to carry an empire's government up to its summer capital.
body: Shimla became the summer capital of British India in 1864, and twice a year the entire government moved between Calcutta and the hills by horse and ox cart. The Kalka–Shimla Railway, built between 1898 and 1903 on narrow 762 mm track, ended that.

From Kalka, at 656 m, the line climbs to Shimla at 2,075 m. It was built with 107 tunnels, of which 102 are still in use; the longest, at Barog, runs for more than a kilometre. There are over 900 curves, the sharpest turning 48 degrees, and several hundred bridges, many of them stone arches stacked like Roman aqueducts.
The ride takes about five hours. In 2008 UNESCO added the line to the Mountain Railways of India World Heritage Site.

stories.title: Across the sea to Rameswaram
stories.dek: India's first sea bridge, and the lift bridge that replaced it in 2025.
body: Rameswaram is on Pamban Island, off the tip of Tamil Nadu. In 1914 a railway bridge was opened across the strait from Mandapam: India's first sea bridge, with a bascule span in the middle that lifted, in two leaves, to let ships through. It survived the 1964 cyclone and carried trains for more than a century, until corrosion closed it for good in December 2022.

Its replacement, the New Pamban Bridge, opened in April 2025 alongside it. It's 2.07 km long and India's first vertical-lift sea bridge: a 72-metre section in the middle rises straight up, level, to let boats pass beneath.
Trains to Rameswaram run from Madurai, Chennai and further afield; the last stretch across the water is the reason to go by rail.

stories.title: Over the Chenab to Kashmir
stories.dek: The world's highest railway bridge, and a line through the Himalayas that took decades to finish.
body: A railway into the Kashmir Valley was planned in the 1970s; its foundation stone was laid in 1983. The last section opened in June 2025, and trains now run from Katra, below the Vaishno Devi shrine, all the way to Srinagar and Baramulla.

The line is a string of superlatives. The Chenab bridge carries it 359 metres above the river bed, higher than the Eiffel Tower, making it the highest railway bridge in the world. Just before it, the Anji Khad bridge is India's first cable-stayed railway bridge, hung from a single 193-metre pylon. Further on, the Pir Panjal tunnel under the mountains between Banihal and Qazigund is more than eleven kilometres long; trains take about nine and a half minutes to pass through.
The Vande Bharat from Katra to Srinagar takes about three hours.

stories.title: Three days on one train
stories.dek: From Assam to the southern tip of India without changing: the Vivek Express.
body: The Vivek Express from Dibrugarh in Assam to Kanniyakumari, the southern tip of the mainland, runs the longest route on Indian Railways: about 4,155 km in a little over three days, with 57 stops in between.

It crosses eight states on the way: Assam, Nagaland, West Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, and passes through Jharkhand without stopping. The route takes in the Brahmaputra plains, the Bengal delta, the length of India's east coast, and Kerala's backwaters before the final run to the cape. The trains were launched in 2013 to mark the 150th birth anniversary of Swami Vivekananda.
The runner-up is almost as epic: the Himsagar Express runs about 3,790 km from Kanniyakumari to Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Katra in Jammu and Kashmir, through twelve states, once a week.

stories.title: The Deccan Queen
stories.dek: Mumbai to Pune since 1930, on the train that has a birthday party.
body: The Deccan Queen first ran on 1 June 1930, as a weekend train for Bombay's well-off heading to the races at Pune. It was, in the words of its own history, India's first superfast train, first long-distance electric train, first vestibuled train, first with a women-only car, and first with a dining car.

Ninety-odd years on it still runs daily between Mumbai CSMT and Pune, climbing the Bhor Ghat, the 1863 line up the Western Ghats with 28 tunnels. Its dining car is part of the legend, and every 1 June its regulars celebrate its birthday on the platform at Pune.

rides.label: The Deccan Queen: Mumbai to Pune

stories.title: Into the Eastern Ghats to Araku
stories.dek: Fifty-eight tunnels between the port of Visakhapatnam and a valley of coffee.
body: The line from Visakhapatnam to Kirandul was built to carry iron ore from the mines of Bastar to the port, climbing through the Eastern Ghats. The Koraput–Araku–Waltair section was completed in 1982.

On the way up to Araku the train threads 58 tunnels and crosses 84 major bridges, with the Borra Caves not far from the line. Araku itself is a valley of coffee estates and tribal villages, cool when the coast is steaming.
The morning passenger from Visakhapatnam takes about four hours to Araku.

stories.title: The first Rajdhani
stories.dek: New Delhi to Howrah in 1969: 1,450 km overnight, and a new idea of fast.
body: In the 1960s, Indian trains were limited to 96 km/h on broad gauge. On 1 March 1969 the first Rajdhani Express, nine coaches, left New Delhi for Howrah, allowed up to 120 km/h, and covered the 1,450 km in 17 hours 20 minutes.
Rajdhani means 'capital'. For three years it was the only one; then the Rajdhanis spread, linking New Delhi with the capitals of the states, fully air-conditioned and given priority on the network.
More than half a century later the New Delhi–Howrah Rajdhani still runs overnight, a little faster.

stories.title: The Kalka Mail, now the Netaji Express
stories.dek: Howrah to Kalka since 1866, and the train Subhas Chandra Bose escaped on.
body: On 1 July 1866 the East Indian Railway started a train to carry British officials, their families and their staff between Calcutta, the capital, and the summer capital in the hills. It became the Kalka Mail, one of the oldest trains still running in India.

On the night of 17 January 1941, Subhas Chandra Bose, under house arrest in Calcutta, slipped away and boarded it at Gomoh, the start of his escape to Peshawar and beyond. On 21 January 2021, for his 125th birth anniversary, the train was renamed the Netaji Express.
It still runs daily between Howrah and Kalka, where the narrow-gauge line to Shimla begins.

stories.title: The Frontier Mail
stories.dek: Ballard Pier to Peshawar, cooled with blocks of ice: now the Golden Temple Mail.
body: Before Partition, passengers arriving in Bombay by steamer from Europe could step off at Ballard Pier and onto the Frontier Mail, bound for Peshawar on the North-West Frontier. It ran under that name from 1928; before air-conditioning, slabs of ice were used to cool its first-class coaches.
In 1996 it was renamed the Golden Temple Mail, after the shrine at its end of the line. It now runs daily between Mumbai (Bandra Terminus) and Amritsar, the fastest daily train between the two.

rides.label: Golden Temple Mail: Mumbai to Amritsar

facts.text: India's first passenger train ran on 16 April 1853: 34 km from Bombay to Thane, 14 carriages carrying about 400 people, pulled by three locomotives named Sahib, Sindh and Sultan.
Eastern India's first passenger train ran on 15 August 1854, from Howrah to Hooghly, 39 km.
South India's first train ran in 1856 from Royapuram in Madras. With the first Bombay and Thane buildings long gone, Royapuram is the oldest railway station still standing in the subcontinent.
The Thane viaducts, built over Thane Creek in 1854 when the first line was extended towards Kalyan, were India's first railway bridges.

The Fairy Queen, built in Leeds in 1855, is listed by Guinness as the world's oldest steam locomotive in regular service. It pulls a two-coach train of 50 passengers, and lives at the Rewari Railway Heritage Museum.
The Kalka Mail started on 1 July 1866 to carry the British government between Calcutta and its summer capital, Shimla. Renamed in 2021, it's now the Netaji Express.
On the night of 17 January 1941, Subhas Chandra Bose boarded the Kalka Mail at Gomoh, escaping house arrest in Calcutta on his way to Peshawar.

Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus was finished in 1887, the year of Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee, and was called Victoria Terminus until 1996. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and still a working station.
The first Rajdhani Express left New Delhi for Howrah on 1 March 1969 and covered 1,450 km in 17 hours 20 minutes. Rajdhani means 'capital'.
'Shatabdi' means 'century': the first Shatabdi Express, New Delhi to Gwalior, was announced in 1988 for the birth centenary of Jawaharlal Nehru.
The first Garib Rath ('chariot of the poor'), air-conditioned travel at lower fares, ran on 5 October 2006 between Saharsa and Amritsar.
The Palace on Wheels, a luxury train modelled on the private trains of India's princely states, was launched on 26 January 1982.
Kolkata Metro opened in 1984, the first rapid transit system in South Asia.
The Deccan Queen, first run on 1 June 1930, was India's first train with a dining car and first with a women-only car. Its regulars still celebrate its birthday at Pune every 1 June.
The Samjhauta Express began on 22 July 1976, after the Simla Agreement, running about 50 km between Amritsar and Lahore.
The Thar Express between Jodhpur and Karachi revived a rail route that had been closed for 41 years when it started in 2006. It has been cancelled since August 2019.
Chittaranjan Locomotive Works turned out its first steam locomotives on 26 January 1950, the day India became a republic.
The Vivek Express from Dibrugarh to Kanniyakumari runs India's longest train route: about 4,155 km, with 57 stops, in a little over three days.
The weekly Himsagar Express runs about 3,790 km from Kanniyakumari to Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Katra, through twelve states.
The first Vande Bharat began carrying passengers on 15 February 2019. The trainsets, built by the Integral Coach Factory in Chennai, reached 183 km/h in trials.
Vande Bharat sleeper trains, with sixteen air-conditioned sleeper coaches, started running in January 2026.
160 km/h is the top speed allowed on Indian Railways, reached by the Gatimaan Express and some Vande Bharats on the Tughlakabad–Agra section.
The Lifeline Express, running since 16 July 1991, was the world's first hospital train: it takes surgery and treatment to rural India by rail.
Before air-conditioning, the Frontier Mail (today's Golden Temple Mail) cooled its first-class coaches with slabs of ice.
The Maharajas' Express was voted the World's Leading Luxury Train at the World Travel Awards seven years in a row, 2012 to 2018.
The WAP-7, at 6,125 horsepower, is the most powerful passenger locomotive on Indian Railways, and the most common.
The Nilgiri Mountain Railway's steam engines climb at about 15 km/h: on the rack section, the toy train to Ooty goes at about the pace of a bicycle.
The Chenab bridge in Jammu and Kashmir carries trains 359 m above the river bed: the highest railway bridge in the world, and taller than the Eiffel Tower. It opened on 6 June 2025.
The Anji Khad bridge, near Reasi, is India's first cable-stayed railway bridge: 96 steel cables hold it from a single 193 m pylon.
Trains take about nine and a half minutes to pass through the Pir Panjal tunnel between Banihal and Qazigund, 11.2 km under the mountains.
The old Pamban bridge to Rameswaram (1914) was India's first sea bridge. Its middle lifted in two leaves to let ships pass.
The New Pamban Bridge, opened in April 2025, is India's first vertical-lift sea bridge: a 72 m span rises straight up to let boats through.
Building the Konkan Railway took more than 2,000 bridges and 92 tunnels along 756 km of coast.
The Kalka–Shimla line was built with 107 tunnels; 102 are still in use. It has more than 900 curves, the sharpest turning 48 degrees.
The Darjeeling toy train climbs by zig-zagging: it runs forward, reverses up the next leg, then runs forward again, gaining height along the hillside.
The Nilgiri Mountain Railway is India's only rack railway: on the steepest stretch the engine pulls itself up by a toothed rail between the running rails.
The Bhor Ghat line up the Western Ghats to Pune opened in 1863 with 28 tunnels.
India's broad gauge, 1,676 mm (5 ft 6 in), is also used in Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Argentina and Chile, and on San Francisco's BART.
About 99% of India's broad-gauge network is electrified (October 2025).
The line from Visakhapatnam to Kirandul through the Eastern Ghats has 58 tunnels and 84 major bridges.
The Kangra Valley Railway, 164 km of narrow gauge from Pathankot into the Himalayan foothills, crosses 950 bridges.
Navapur station sits on the Gujarat–Maharashtra border.
Bhawani Mandi's platform is in two states: its northern end in Madhya Pradesh, its southern end in Rajasthan.
Ib, in Odisha, has the shortest station name on Indian Railways, after the Ib river. Coal was discovered by accident there in 1900, while the railway was building a bridge.
Chennai Central's official name since 2019, Puratchi Thalaivar Dr. M.G. Ramachandran Central, is the longest station name on Indian Railways, and second in the world only to Llanfair… in Wales.
Venkatanarasimharajuvaripeta, on the Andhra Pradesh–Tamil Nadu border, has India's second-longest station name. Express trains don't stop there.
Platform 1 at Hubballi Junction is 1,507 metres long: the longest railway platform in the world.
Ghum, on the Darjeeling toy train line, is India's highest railway station at 2,260 m.
Howrah is India's largest railway complex: 23 platforms, and every day about 250 long-distance trains and 500 suburban ones.
Kanniyakumari is the southernmost railway station on the Indian mainland.
Lucknow's Charbagh station, finished in 1923, is one of India's grandest Indo-Saracenic buildings.
Indian Railways runs about 13,000 passenger trains a day, stopping at some 7,300 stations; in 2023–24 it carried 6.9 billion passengers.
India's railway is the fourth-largest national network in the world: 69,181 km of routes and more than 135,000 km of track.
With more than 1.2 million employees, Indian Railways is one of the ten biggest employers in the world.
Mumbai's suburban trains carry more than 7.5 million people a day, on over 2,300 services.
Patiala had a steam-hauled monorail from 1907 to 1927: the only locomotive-hauled railway ever built on the Ewing system. One of its engines is at the National Rail Museum in New Delhi.
Begunkodor station in West Bengal was abandoned for 42 years after tales of a ghost on the platform in 1967. It reopened in 2009.
Indian Railways' mascot is Bholu, an elephant train guard holding a signal lamp, unveiled in 2002 for the railways' 150th anniversary.
Some tourist brochures call Ghum the highest railway station in the world. It never was: Tanggula, on the line to Lhasa in Tibet, is at 5,068 m.
The Konkan coast was first surveyed for a railway in 1920. The line opened 78 years later, in 1998.
You can see Dudhsagar Falls, 310 m high, from the train between Goa and Belagavi: the line crosses right in front of them.
Before the Darjeeling railway opened in 1881, the journey from Kolkata to Darjeeling took five to six days, the last stretch by bullock cart and palanquin.
